You wear your dress up to here, so when you sit down, you just barely cover your booty and you're sexy and you have your breasts added to and you lay around and if a baby comes and you don't want to be bothered, you have it aborted. This is the way we live. You don't owe anybody anything. All you're supposed to do is have some money and blame a man for everything low that ever happened to you. Yeah. It's a disgusting world. Mm-hmm. These are the singers. What are they going to say? A lot of people made money on Billie Holliday after she died. A lot of young singers. They didn't have the slightest idea as to who Billie Holliday was and sang some of her songs and put the flower in their hair, but they're not doing that right now. Aretha Franklin started with reverence. That's how she got the music. There's a bunch of little scallywags and they imitate people, but they don't have anything to bring us. They don't have anything to give us. They don't even have a sound of their own and they have no morality. A lot of people have lost the sense of morality and principle. It embarrasses them to talk about it. I think the devil came and got the world, if you want to know what I think, finally. It came and it belongs to the devil, to the lie. You're not supposed to know anything, but things change. It's not a time of great performers. They're in the past. Great individual stylists. Oh, that's so and so. I wish -- I mean, I don't hear that.
Do you see any young artists that you think can keep the tradition?

I think a lot of the young men are doing this. I haven't heard anybody who reminds me -- not do songs like Dinah Washington, but who -- you know what I mean? Ella Fitzgerald or Sarah or -- I haven't heard anybody yet. Cassandra Wilson has a song and Diane Reeves, but I'm talking about -- I don't know. It's like the brilliance of Charlie Parker, and I should be the last one because I'm a late-bloomer myself. I didn't get it all at once. But they are really fine singers, but somebody who is from another dimension, maybe. You know what I mean? We haven't seen anything like that here. Maybe it's the times. So mediocre, yeah, right now. Mediocrity is the -- whew! The active 30 years ago were brilliant. I'm telling you. I mean, a lot of the folks that are here, I don't even know who they are. Maybe it's me, maybe it's me. I don't know them and they don't leave an impression on me. I think it's like a non-entity and they make a lot of money. Maybe that's what it is. I think that the industry bought the souls of the people. They offered them a lot of money and so they'll just do anything. Models that look like tarts. There used to be street walkers dressed like that, exposing themselves, and in the name of these so-called great designers.

Could be great themselves. I wonder why the feminists don't say anything about that. I don't get it. Why she wouldn't say what are you doing to us? Why don't you have a decent garment for a woman to wear? Half of her behind exposed. It's embarrassing. This is not about the music, right?
Well, it's part of it. It's the business and it's the image, but -­
Yeah.

-- you're talking about feminists objecting to that. What about this more sort of interpretation of the music now from different perspectives, of women's history in jazz from more feminists' perspective?

Women don't have a history in jazz. That's just a lot of garbage the feminists have brought to us. Listen, women have the same history in jazz as they do in classical music. Does she -- is she the composer? Does she conduct the orchestra? She sings, just like they do in this form. If we depended on women to bring music, we'd be in trouble. They don't bring music. They bring babies. They become famous being married to a man. It's a rare woman, like Melba Liston, who comes to the music for the music. Rare. Hazel Scott.
Why do you think that is?

Because they're women and they make babies. A man doesn't make a child. He doesn't clone a human being. His work is all cut out for him. She makes the people and he makes the world that they come into. What's wrong with this? Why is it all of a sudden she wants to pretend that she's something that she's not? She doesn't build bridges. It's not because the men didn't let her build one. Her mind is not there. This is not who a woman is. I know, I'm a woman. Women do not think along these terms. It's a rare woman who does. Freud was a man. Everybody who's impacted on the world, on the outside world, it's the women who bring the men and women here and teach them what she knows. What kind of a woman brings a man who's a male chauvinist? What did she teach him when he's a child? She suckles him at her breast and she brings her own worst enemy here? Is this a man's fault or hers? I think we need to look at this. I'm tired of this feminist crap. How are you going to be a feminist and you bring men and women here? What about the boy? Doesn't his life mean anything? What's he going to do while you're being a feminist? What about being a humanist? What's wrong with that? No, I have no sympathy for them, I mean, and I think they're really taking disadvantage and the men who were called male chauvinists are really pushovers because he gives her anything she asks for. She doesn't make me feel safe walking around with her dress up

just below her behind. What kind of a woman is this? Old women in their underwear they call tights. Really? Where's her dress? A man is made to look at a woman and become excited. He has to have an erection. There's a difference between men and women. She doesn't have to have anything to make the baby. She doesn't have to feel anything, but he has to have an erection. So, what is this? And she jumps on the man and pretends that she's hot in the first kiss. What happened to foreplay? What about the little girls who are coming through, who are being assaulted by men who don't know how to treat a girl anymore? In these movies that they make with them coming at each other with their mouths open in the heat of passion for the first kiss. Give me a break. These are a bunch of frigid people who don't feel anything. Otherwise they wouldn't approach a human being like that. I am female. There's nothing greater than being female, but I'm not greater than a man and a man is not greater than me. No, I'm not a feminist. She preempted the black movement, the feminist did. She got jobs that she never would have had before. The Secretary of State and the prosecuting attorney. When is it going to be my turn? It's two for her and none for me. The designers make clothes for women that they have no respect for. They don't even finish the garment anymore. They charge you an arm and a leg for something. You can see it in the style what these men think of these women and the men are the ones who design our clothes. Men design our clothes. I don't care what he does in this world. He dresses himself and he wears his clothes. I'm glad you gave me a chance to get that off.
Me, too.
It drives me crazy.
What would you say to young artists or young people who want to find their voice, to find their own spirit the way that you found your own?

Well, it sounds real simple and I think it really is, but it's not really that simple. Mama taught me this and I wrote this song and I said that she did. Mama told me of a beauty that is made of purest gold, one the weather will not tarnish, one that never will grow old. She said beauty comes from understanding, looking at the things we see, beauty of the human spirit, beauty that will set us free. I think that's really everything. To see your inherent beauty that was given you free, gratis, by that that made us, the ability to think and make choices, and if you find yourself beautiful, you can't find anybody else not beautiful. That's the thing. It takes one to know one. So, I'm glad. I find that -- I believe that my ancestors were beautiful and somehow that is who God is. I don't know what God is, other than that that made me and who wrote stories a long time ago and told me who I was and where I was. Yeah. The artists, I think

they're the most powerful people on the planet. They always have been. The artists and the scientists, the people who think and steer the course here. Those are the most powerful people in the world who have ever been on the planet. So, I would say look for understanding. If you know who you are, you can control your life, no matter what anybody else says, you know. Somebody else's opinion doesn't mean anything, but I live on a planet and I know that the sun isn't out all the time. This is constant. There's darkness and there's light and we have no power here. If the elements come to get us, there's nothing we can do about it. It's always been like that. When the folks went to discover Egypt and Rome and Greece, they found it under sand, didn't they? When the archaeologists -- wasn't it under sand? People don't just -- I mean, cities don't just gather sand. Something has to happen and you never know when destruction will come. I believe that destruction is the beginning of something. I believe that the phoenix rises from the ashes and all that stuff. I do. It all sounds real to me. I believe that God is great, whatever it is, and our ancestors said that there was such a thing, that we are made like this. We are made perfect and whole and we can do anything we want to do, but you have to reach for understanding and you're not supposed to be a sucker here.
How about telling us a little bit about the autobiography you're working on?

Yes, I've been working on it for 20 or 25 years and I don't have a title for it yet, the autobiography, but I want to tell a story that will describe for youngsters what is before them when they say they want to come to the stage. I want to talk about a country and a world that is difficult sometimes to live in. Well, I said this before, but I would like it to be just to approach Charlotte Bronte's "Jane Eyre." With "Jane Eyre," you knew in that story, you knew who the English were, what they were socially, who they were socially, how they felt about things. That's what I'd like to write, a story that tells about a world and a people, and to show somehow the value of the work, the value of the music, to be somebody great, like Duke Ellington who's got a street named for him just two blocks up the street. Mm-hmm. Other than that, and I looked forward. This is my 66th year. If I live to be a hundred, I'm more than halfway through it, you know. I don't want to live to be a hundred, but I'd -­ well, I look forward to eventually to the transition, to that thing that happens for all of us. We don't have to stay here forever, and I'd like to leave everything intact. Hopefully somebody will find it useful, the thoughts that I have. I always -- all my life, they told me when I was a young girl, Anna Marie, you talk too much. When I became Abbey Lincoln, Abby, you talk too much. Well, I'm still talking.
Is there anything that you hope people will take from this autobiography?

I don't care. It's for my sake. It's for the sake of my own life. I gave the best I had. If they got something from it, it's okay. I didn't make the world. I'm not God alone. It's okay with me. Just as long as I get a chance to express it, I don't have to swallow it down. If I can say it, it's enough for me. I don't believe that it was left up to me to save the world. I wouldn't know what to save it from or how to save it anyway, but I have a right to sing my songs.
(END OF AUDIO FILE)

segments.title: Opening of the third interview
segments.summary: Sally Plaxson welcomes Abbey Lincoln to their third interview and proposes starting at the beginning.

segments.title: Family ancestry: slave grandparents and the Wooldridge line
segments.summary: Her mother told the family history: grandparents born into slavery, a grandfather in a degraded state, a Wooldridge grandfather who killed two men, and a family of about 150 descendants.

segments.title: Where the family walked from, and her grandmother's many births
segments.summary: Asked where they started, she recalls her mother's tales of the Civil War and of her own mother's 17 births, and her father midwifing the last six.

segments.title: Her grandmother the teacher and a humble family life
segments.summary: Her grandmother taught her mother and father to read, did laundry, and the family was poor but proud; her brothers later became businessmen.

segments.title: Naming her brothers and sisters
segments.summary: She lists the siblings from Nellie and Evelyn to Shirley the baby, and says her mother kept incest in the family history before them.

segments.title: Her mother and father's stormy marriage
segments.summary: Her mother was a principled, independent woman who fought back; her father liked street life and built everything himself.

segments.title: Her mother's religion and the Psalms
segments.summary: Her mother studied Christian Science and took the children to the AME church, and taught Abbey the Psalms she still recites.

segments.title: Early Chicago memory: the lawnmower accident
segments.summary: Her one memory of Chicago is putting her hand into a lawnmower.

segments.title: Why the family moved to the country; her father's work
segments.summary: Her mother, jealous of her fast father, nagged him into moving out of the city; he was a handyman, and her parents had little schooling.

segments.title: Depression, her parents' separation and her brothers' enlistment
segments.summary: The family nearly starved in Calvin Center, Michigan, after her mother left her father, survived on rabbits and relief, and the brothers enlisted.

segments.title: Calvin Center community, one-room school and first piano
segments.summary: She describes the olive-skinned community, the general store jukebox, the one-room school and picking out melodies on the piano at five.

segments.title: Her father singing to the baby and her mother's church voice
segments.summary: Her father sang to baby Shirley by the stove, and her mother's rugged church voice is the sound Abbey inherited.

segments.title: Church songs, Kalamazoo radio and high-school band follies
segments.summary: She played church songs on the piano, then learned radio songs and sang at band follies for Mr. Chinnery, seeing Lionel Hampton and Ella Fitzgerald, and criticizes church imagery.

segments.title: Victrola records and the ugly comic recordings of her childhood
segments.summary: She had no blues records, only her father's victrola with comic race records she remembers with distaste.

segments.title: Hearing Billie Holiday and Coleman Hawkins at fourteen
segments.summary: Her sister brought home Hawkins's 'Body and Soul' and a Billie Holiday record that changed her life; radio then offered all kinds of singers.

segments.title: Mother leaves the farm for Kalamazoo and segregated high school
segments.summary: After the separation her mother moved the family to Kalamazoo, where Abbey attended the hilltop high school while living in servants' quarters.

segments.title: Making her own clothes and wearing her hair as a teenager
segments.summary: She sewed outfits from scraps, wore riding boots and ribbons, and became notorious for her style while being told her hair was no good.

segments.title: Failing school music but singing solo for Mr. Chinnery
segments.summary: She failed music and arts and stayed in school for the yearly show; after graduating she was singing with Benny Poole's band in Jackson.

segments.title: Reverend Smith, Jackson, Benny Poole and day work
segments.summary: The minister invited her to sing in Jackson where she met Benny Poole's musicians, while working as a domestic and being fired by a doctor's wife.

segments.title: Radio and visiting artists around Kalamazoo
segments.summary: She heard records on the radio and sometimes sang with visiting acts like Wardell Gray, but did not grow up with theater.

segments.title: Not knowing jazz; being introduced to Charlie Parker
segments.summary: She knew only singers' names, and recalls the piano player making her introduction to Bird unfollowable.

segments.chapter: Road work, Honolulu and a new name
segments.title: Moving to California and the Salt Lake City piano player
segments.summary: She went to California at 20, was booked by agent Johnnie Robinson, and was shoved to the floor by a piano player after a rehearsal argument in Salt Lake City.

segments.chapter: Road work, Honolulu and a new name
segments.title: The poem 'On Being High' and teaching in Los Angeles
segments.summary: She recites her 1970 poem about abuse and surviving as a pretty young woman, and mentions lecturing and teaching Pan-African studies.

segments.chapter: Road work, Honolulu and a new name
segments.title: Finishing the job on crutches as Anna Marie
segments.summary: The pianist's wife apologized, and Abbey worked on crutches since she could not afford a doctor, billed as the lovely Anna Marie.

segments.chapter: Road work, Honolulu and a new name
segments.title: Non-musical dues: corruption in Honolulu
segments.summary: Asked about non-musical struggles, she describes the corrupt Honolulu scene, where musicians were prostitutes and addicts, and her mother's teaching protected her.

segments.chapter: Road work, Honolulu and a new name
segments.title: Honolulu clubs and the drug bust
segments.summary: She names the Tradewinds, Brown Derby and Lolly Chi's, the stars who came through, and the band's addictions and the federal bust in 1952-53.

segments.title: How Anna Marie became Abbey Lincoln
segments.summary: Back from Honolulu in 1954 she worked the LeMadeline, met Eddie Beal and Bob Russell, was called Gaby at the Moulin Rouge, and Russell gave her the name Abbey Lincoln.

segments.title: One person, many names: Anna Marie, Abbey and Aminata
segments.summary: She says all her names are the same one, and describes the African name Aminata given in Guinea and Moseka from Zaire.

segments.title: Rehearsing with Eddie Beal and learning to sing sincerely
segments.summary: Beal coached her to sing songs as written and drop borrowed habits from Sarah Vaughan and Dinah Washington.

segments.title: Singers who all sound alike, and the film The Girl Can't Help It
segments.summary: She says modern singers sound alike, then recounts Bob Russell arranging her song in The Girl Can't Help It in a Marilyn Monroe dress and the publicity afterward.

segments.title: Max Roach saves her from the image; her first album Affair
segments.summary: Max told her she did not have to do this; her first album, Affair, with Benny Carter arrangements of Bob Russell songs, came out on Liberty with a provocative cover.

segments.title: Never wanting to be a star
segments.summary: She says she never wished to be a movie star and only dreamed of a man who would save her.

segments.title: The voice as the original instrument and the singer as storyteller
segments.summary: She argues the voice is superior to horns, that scatting follows telling the story, and that there is no such thing as jazz, only song and spirit.

segments.title: Billie, Sarah and the queens left only footprints
segments.summary: The great women singers were unapproachable, and she would never have asked them for lessons.

segments.title: Seeing Billie Holiday in Honolulu
segments.summary: She saw Billie twice in Honolulu with her Chihuahuas and never spoke to her, and contrasts that reverence with today's singers.

segments.title: Jam sessions, building a reputation without management
segments.summary: She sat in at jam spots, believes reputation is built where you are, and says stardom only meant she could get a job.

segments.chapter: Road work, Honolulu and a new name
segments.title: Johnnie Griffin, Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington
segments.summary: In Honolulu Johnnie Griffin sat in and shamed her saxophonist; she praises Armstrong and Duke Ellington as great, respectful men.

segments.chapter: Road work, Honolulu and a new name
segments.title: The Honolulu bands: Rampart Streeters and Blinkie Allen
segments.summary: She names the groups she worked with, then the Say When Club in San Francisco where the owner ran off with Nellie Lutcher's money.

segments.chapter: Road work, Honolulu and a new name
segments.title: Rhythm and blues repertoire before she knew bebop
segments.summary: Everyone knew Percy Mayfield and Louis Jordan; she had not yet met Dizzy Gillespie or Roach.

segments.title: Making the first album: Bob Russell and picking her songs
segments.summary: Bob Russell arranged for Benny Carter and Marty Paich; she chose the songs and built the album around a love story gone bad, though she was not yet writing.

segments.title: Las Vegas and Caesars Palace
segments.summary: She hated Las Vegas, was fired at Caesars Palace after singing Coltrane's 'Africa' lyric, and joked about being Lincoln's illegitimate daughter.

segments.title: When she began writing: Abbey's Blue and Monk's endorsement
segments.summary: She wrote 'Let Up' for Abbey's Blue, added lyrics to Monk and Coltrane tunes, and began writing seriously after Monk called her a composer.

segments.title: Writing process and the artist's role in civilization
segments.summary: She usually hears words first, researched the world from old encyclopedias in 1970, and says civilizations live through artists.

segments.title: The new song, men and women in jazz, and Max's lesson on the beat
segments.summary: She recites a new song, argues men bring the music, recalls Max Roach teaching her to sing on the beat, and praises the music's range.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: Arriving in New York's circle of young artists
segments.summary: In New York she met Maya Angelou, John Killens and Monk, began thinking of herself as part of a people, and wore her hair natural.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: The Down Beat critic and becoming socially conscious
segments.summary: Critics called her a professional Negro for her protest songs, and she reflects on stopping 'When Malindy Sings' and on blame and victimhood.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: Max Roach's crowd and what a bandleader passes on
segments.summary: Max took Julian Priester and Booker Little under his wing, which she says is the test of a bandleader.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: Not a musical school but a social philosophy
segments.summary: She says her New York years were less about musical learning than a social philosophy that gave her new concerns.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: How the Freedom Now Suite came about and learning to scream
segments.summary: Oscar Brown Jr. and Max Roach conceived the suite; Max's nephew Darryl taught her to scream for 'Protest'.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: Riverside albums, In the Red, Jamaica and Straight Ahead
segments.summary: She recounts That's Him, the early reputation as loony, the stage musical Jamaica, and writing Straight Ahead with Mal Waldron.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: The Down Beat attack and the masochist image of black women
segments.summary: She quotes her defense of singing about freedom, and says black women singers were stereotyped as masochists.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: Living and writing with Max
segments.summary: In lean times she and Max wrote at the piano, and she learned composition from him and heard his Charlie Parker stories.

segments.title: Who manipulates the images of women singers
segments.summary: She blames the industry for degrading images, rap and sexual songs.

segments.title: Becoming an artist and a writer
segments.summary: She says meeting other artists, especially Oscar Brown and Maya Angelou, made her see herself as a writer.

segments.title: What she is leaving behind
segments.summary: She hopes her best understanding endures and calls herself a late bloomer.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: Odd meters: Max Roach and five-four time
segments.summary: Max introduced five-four in Chicago with the Turrentines and Booker Little, and Brubeck's band heard it.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: Learning to sing in five-four
segments.summary: She learned the odd meters by listening to Max and experimented with Booker Little's dissonant arrangement of 'In the Red'.

segments.title: A lifetime of learning and the lyric to 'Lonesome Lover'
segments.summary: She says her years of experience prepared her, and how she wrote the lyric to Max's 'Lonesome Lover'.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: 'Naturally' and the Afro in 1962
segments.summary: She wrote 'Naturally' to encourage women about their hair, performed it in Harlem hair shows in the early 1960s.

segments.chapter: New York and the Freedom Now years
segments.title: Writing lyrics to other composers' music
segments.summary: She wrote lyrics to Guy Warren, Villa-Lobos, Monk and Coltrane tunes, sometimes without permission, which later caused trouble with their families.

segments.title: Leaving New York, Miriam Makeba's trip to Africa, and men and women
segments.summary: After leaving her marriage and career for Los Angeles, Miriam Makeba took her to Guinea in 1973 where she was named Aminata.

segments.title: Music in Africa and Liberia
segments.summary: She heard only Miriam and Hugh Masekela, visited Liberia before its fall, and felt at home but universal.

segments.title: NAACP, CORE, the Muslims and Freedom Now concerts
segments.summary: The NAACP disliked them; they performed the suite for several groups and Malcolm X as fundraisers.

segments.title: Africa did not awaken her
segments.summary: She says she was awake before Africa and feels no more partial to it than to Europe.

segments.title: Black Power, the avant garde and money
segments.summary: She thinks Coltrane's 'Africa' had little effect and that she and Max were not rich, but says she feels grateful.

segments.title: The spirit that uses the instrument
segments.summary: The next session on voice and spirit: it is the spirit, not the instrument, that makes the sound.

segments.title: Her birthday, youth and the child spirit
segments.summary: Born August 6, 1930, she talks about children being told to sit down and shut up.

segments.title: 'Playmate' and the spirit that visits
segments.summary: The song 'Playmate' came as a visiting thought, and the spirit has grown stronger, as with 'Cage Bird'.

segments.title: Einstein and the arts and sciences
segments.summary: She talks of Einstein, saying artists and scientists make human life possible.

segments.title: Monk: 'Don't be so perfect' at the Straight Ahead session
segments.summary: Monk told her not to be perfect; she recalls the Candid session with Hawkins, Booker Little, Mal Waldron, and Max.

segments.title: Taking risks as an artist
segments.summary: She says she never took risks as an artist, and was not born with a career.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Second day of the interview
segments.summary: Plaxson notes the date is December 18, 1996.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Coming to New York: the Village Vanguard and seeing Lena Horne
segments.summary: She describes the New York clubs and seeing Lena Horne at the Waldorf-Astoria, which changed her life.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Arriving in New York and Central Park West
segments.summary: She never dreamed of New York; she worked with Cab Calloway in the park and met the Rat Pack.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: The Village Vanguard dressing room and jazz club conditions
segments.summary: She resents jazz rooms with no dressing rooms and treatment of musicians.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Same conditions in Europe
segments.summary: Clubs in Europe follow the same tradition, even in basement bomb shelters.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: The ideal room is a concert hall
segments.summary: She prefers concert halls like Carnegie Hall over smoky clubs.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: The black community does not support the music
segments.summary: She says the black community, press and record companies ignore jazz.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Jazz rooms as brothels and why they are not romantic
segments.summary: She argues jazz joints are poverty, and musicians make the rooms famous.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Big bands, dancing and the concert hall
segments.summary: People now listen rather than dance, and she says that is not why the music is poorly presented.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: No support from her own people: Apollo and Harlem
segments.summary: She criticizes the lack of support from black institutions and Harlem and says artists go to Europe.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: The Pacific Northwest circuit and agent Johnnie Robinson
segments.summary: She describes the circuit through Salt Lake City, Roseburg and Honolulu booked by Robinson.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Traveling cheaply and what she earned
segments.summary: She went by bus and car, earned $100 a week in Honolulu, and says the people make musicians rich.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Traveling with her own band after the film
segments.summary: After the film she traveled to Canada, England and Sweden, then insisted on great musicians from her first Max Roach album.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Playing for white audiences, trios and the Harlem club Wells
segments.summary: She was often the only black person, then worked with a piano player and later a trio at Wells.

segments.title: Audiences and commanding the stage
segments.summary: She learned from Sarah and Billie that the stage is a provisional government, and tells of a noisy Philadelphia club.

segments.title: Stage fright and preparation
segments.summary: She suffered stage fright at Ceros and Max told her he was too busy preparing.

segments.title: A female God and Moseka
segments.summary: She explains her female god and the name Moseka.

segments.title: Acting and its effect on her singing
segments.summary: She credits her film directors and acting as part of being a storyteller.

segments.title: The hats and black clothing
segments.summary: She started wearing hats after losing her sister in 1989 and her own illness, as comfort and protection.

segments.title: Jean-Philippe Allard and signing with Verve
segments.summary: Allard called from Paris in 1989 and signed her for three albums, after major American labels ignored her.

segments.title: How she works with Allard
segments.summary: Like Max, Allard suggests musicians like Hank Jones and Pat Metheny while she picks songs.

segments.title: Enja album with Steve Coleman and the Sweet Basil dressing room
segments.summary: In 1984 Steve Coleman sat in at Sweet Basil's and brought her a band for the Enja album.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: The Newport protest and sick, crazy musicians
segments.summary: She recalls Roach, Mingus and Max Gordon's festival protest and the East 74th Street Theater.

segments.chapter: Venues, circuits and the music business
segments.title: Beatles pay, jazz pay and money
segments.summary: She compares the Beatles' pay with Miles Davis's weekly pay and says she doesn't miss money.

segments.title: Her hair and the poem 'The Coiled Strand'
segments.summary: She recites her 1970 poem and criticizes Michael Jackson's changes.

segments.title: Poetry, painting and 'Echang'
segments.summary: She writes poems and paints to heal, and found the word Echang, meaning throw it away.

segments.title: Moments that changed her life: Monk and Roach's order
segments.summary: She learned from Roach the principle of order.

segments.title: The film Nothing But a Man
segments.summary: She discusses Michael Roemer's film, her role as a schoolteacher, and its reception.

segments.title: For Love of Ivy with Sidney Poitier
segments.summary: She describes how she got the role opposite Poitier.

segments.title: Painting and writing in Los Angeles after 1970
segments.summary: She started painting and writing her own songs, made People in Me in Japan, and dismissed peers.

segments.title: The song 'When I'm Called Home'
segments.summary: She is not conscious of using trials but recounts writing the song on a flight to Japan.

segments.title: Music as healing
segments.summary: She says music honors the gods and that she sings in praise of her ancestors.

segments.title: Options for young female singers
segments.summary: She criticizes the sexualized image of young singers.

segments.title: Young artists who might carry the tradition
segments.summary: She hasn't heard anyone with the individuality of the past.

segments.title: Women in jazz and feminism
segments.summary: She rejects feminism, saying women don't have a history in jazz.

segments.title: Advice to young artists
segments.summary: She says to see your inherent beauty and that artists are powerful.

segments.title: Her autobiography and closing
segments.summary: She talks about her long-running autobiography and says she has a right to sing her songs.
